ddx.step1_summary: Chief complaint: Lower abdominal pain for 2 days with feeling hot/sweaty. Symptoms: midline lower abdominal pain, associated mild nausea, no vomiting; slight pink blood in urine; increased urinary frequency; he also reports being thirstier than normal. No significant past medical history. Allergies: amoxicillin. Medications: none regularly; contraceptive implant in place for one year. Family/social: mother with breast cancer (history noted); lives with parents; non-smoker, drinks alcohol ~4 beers per week. Vital signs/exam: Temp ~37°C (not febrile); no explicit signs of severe illness described; no back pain or vaginal discharge noted; no dysuria reported as present by patient, but occasional difficulty passing urine noted in conversation. Labs/imaging: none mentioned. Risk factors discussed by clinician included possible urinary tract infection. The clinician proposed a 3-day course of antibiotics if infection suspected and advised re-evaluation if symptoms worsen or new symptoms develop.

V: Ureteric/renal colic (kidney stone) – lower abdominal pain with hematuria (pink urine) and nausea; stone can irritate the urinary tract leading to frequency and discomfort.
I: Acute cystitis (lower UTI) – urinary frequency, mild discomfort/difficulty with urination, pink-tinged urine, symptomatic improvement with antibiotics potential.
Pyelonephritis – infection extending to the upper tract is possible but less likely given absence of fever, flank pain, or systemic illness in the transcript.
N: Bladder tumor (neoplasm) – hematuria could occur, but patient is young with acute presentation and no risk factors; lower likelihood.
D: Diabetes mellitus, new-onset (endocrine/metabolic) – polyuria and polydipsia reported; dehydration signs (hot/sweaty) could align with hyperglycemia; needs consideration as contributing or primary issue.
I2: Drug/iatrogenic effects – amoxicillin allergy present; however, current symptoms are not explained by a known adverse drug reaction to amoxicillin.
C: Congenital urinary tract anomalies (e.g., vesicoureteral reflux) – could predispose to UTIs, but no specific history of congenital issues provided.
A: Autoimmune/Interstitial inflammatory conditions (e.g., interstitial cystitis) – possible cause of pelvic pain, but less supported by the acute hematuria and infection-intuition.
T: Traumatic injury to abdomen/pelvis – not described in the transcript.
E: Endocrine/metabolic disorders (diabetes mellitus) – recurrent polyuria and polydipsia with dehydration could indicate metabolic cause.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Acute uncomplicated cystitis (lower urinary tract infection)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Symptoms fit a lower UTI pattern: increased urinary frequency, mild urinary discomfort, and gross/microscopic blood in urine. Clinician considered UTI and offered a 3-day antibiotic course; other red flags are not emphasized.
supporting_evidence: Mild nausea without vomiting; no high fever reported
opposing_evidence: Pain described as lower abdominal rather than classic suprapubic pain; no explicit dysuria reported by patient
